hypothesis: Naturalised alien floras record far more European-native species naturalised in Argentina/Uruguay (La Plata) and, to a lesser degree, in Australia, than southern-hemisphere-native species naturalised in Europe.
pass_criterion: Using GloNAF taxon-by-region lists with native ranges added from a standard checklist: (a) N_EU->LP, the count of naturalised taxa in Argentina plus Uruguay with a native range including Europe, is at least 5 times N_S->EU, the count of naturalised taxa in European regions with a native range wholly in the southern hemisphere; (b) N_EU->AU, the same count for Australia, is at least 2 times N_S->EU but less than N_EU->LP as a share of the recipient flora; (c) southern-origin taxa are under 5% of all taxa naturalised in Europe. All three must hold.
fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if N_EU->LP / N_S->EU is below 3, or N_EU->AU / N_S->EU is below 1.5, or southern-origin taxa make up 10% or more of the taxa naturalised in Europe. Results between these bounds are inconclusive.
interpretation: 'Naturalised' maps to GloNAF's status of naturalised (self-sustaining populations, not merely casual). 'Europe' means GloNAF regions in European countries. 'La Plata' means Argentina plus Uruguay, because GloNAF regions are national or subnational and no La Plata region exists. 'Southern forms' means taxa whose entire native range lies south of the equator. 'Very many... cover the ground' and 'beaten the natives' are not directly measurable. They are reduced to counts and shares of naturalised taxa, with no test of displacement. 'Extremely few' is operationalised as under 5% of Europe's naturalised flora. Native ranges are not part of GloNAF and must be joined from an external checklist such as POWO. The modern data may show more southern taxa in Europe than Darwin knew of, for example Oxalis and Australian acacias, and that is a legitimate reason for the claim to fail.

dataset.name: Global Naturalized Alien Flora (GloNAF)
dataset.publisher: GloNAF consortium (van Kleunen, Pyšek, Dawson, Essl et al.)
dataset.why_it_fits: GloNAF lists naturalised vascular plant taxa for more than 1,000 regions worldwide, including Argentina, Uruguay, Australia and the European countries. Fields used: taxon name, region, and naturalisation status. Native ranges would be joined by taxon name from an external checklist. This allows a reciprocal comparison of north-to-south and south-to-north naturalisation counts.
